title: The zero-g indicator
hook: Many crews carry a small plush toy to tell them the moment they reach orbit.
peek: Strapped into their seats in bulky suits, astronauts cannot easily feel the instant they become weightless. So many crews hang a small soft toy in the cabin. When it starts to float, everyone knows they have made it to space.
lede: During launch, astronauts are pressed into their seats, gloved, helmeted and busy. Reaching weightlessness is a big moment, but it can be hard to notice through all that gear. The answer is charmingly simple: a small plush toy on a tether, hanging in view. While the engines push, it hangs tight. When they cut off and the toy drifts up, the crew is in free fall.

bullets.text: Russian Soyuz crews have used soft toys this way for decades, often dangling them from a string above the seats. The toy is frequently chosen by a crew member's child, which gives it a personal meaning.

On SpaceX's first crewed flight in 2020, astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley carried Tremor, a sparkly sequined dinosaur picked by their young sons. It spent two months on the space station with them before flying home.
When NASA's uncrewed Artemis I mission flew around the Moon in 2022, its zero-g indicator was a small Snoopy in an orange spacesuit, nodding to Snoopy's long history as a NASA mascot.
A soft toy is light, safe to bump into and easy to see on the cabin cameras, so people watching from the ground can see the moment of weightlessness too.
